title: How do you map a domain name to a load balancer (Route 53 alias record vs CNAME), and why prefer an alias record for an AWS resource?
shortTitle: Mapping a Domain to a Load Balancer — Alias Record vs CNAME

s1_definition.profdef: To point a domain at an AWS load balancer you create a DNS record in Route 53 that targets the load balancer's DNS name. You have two choices. A CNAME record maps one domain name to another domain name, so the resolver must do a second lookup to get the IP, and a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex (the naked `example.com`). A Route 53 alias record is an AWS-specific extension that maps a name directly to an AWS resource such as an Application Load Balancer; it resolves to the load balancer's IP addresses inside Route 53, can be used at the zone apex, follows the load balancer's changing IPs automatically, and incurs no charge for alias queries to AWS resources.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine `bank.example.com` is the public name of National Bank of India. A CNAME is like telling a customer "to reach the internet banking desk, first call the central directory, and they will give you another number to call for the load balancer, and only then will you reach a counter." It is an extra hop. An alias record is like the directory knowing the actual counters directly, so when Rajesh asks for internet banking it gives him the real counter numbers in one step, and if the bank adds or removes counters, the directory is updated automatically behind the scenes.
s1_definition.oneliner: A CNAME points a name to another name with an extra lookup and cannot sit at the root domain, while a Route 53 alias points straight to the AWS resource's IPs at the root domain, for free, and tracks its changing addresses automatically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To point a domain at an AWS load balancer you create a DNS record in Route 53 that targets the load balancer's DNS name. You have two choices. A CNAME record maps one domain name to another domain name, so the resolver must do a second lookup to get the IP, and a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex (the naked `example.com`). A Route 53 alias record is an AWS-specific extension that maps a name directly to an AWS resource such as an Application Load Balancer; it resolves to the load balancer's IP addresses inside Route 53, can be used at the zone apex, follows the load balancer's changing IPs automatically, and incurs no charge for alias queries to AWS resources.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine `bank.example.com` is the public name of National Bank of India. A CNAME is like telling a customer "to reach the internet banking desk, first call the central directory, and they will give you another number to call for the load balancer, and only then will you reach a counter." It is an extra hop. An alias record is like the directory knowing the actual counters directly, so when Rajesh asks for internet banking it gives him the real counter numbers in one step, and if the bank adds or removes counters, the directory is updated automatically behind the scenes.

**One line to remember:** A CNAME points a name to another name with an extra lookup and cannot sit at the root domain, while a Route 53 alias points straight to the AWS resource's IPs at the root domain, for free, and tracks its changing addresses automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
A load balancer in AWS does not give you a fixed IP address for an Application Load Balancer; it gives you a DNS name like `my-alb-123456.ap-south-1.elb.amazonaws.com`, and the IP addresses behind that name change over time as AWS scales the load balancer. So you must map your friendly domain to that name, not to an IP.

With a CNAME record, you tell DNS that `www.bank.example.com` is an alias for `my-alb-123456.ap-south-1.elb.amazonaws.com`. When a client resolves `www.bank.example.com`, the resolver gets the CNAME, then does a second resolution of the load balancer's name to finally get an IP. This works, but it has two limits. First, DNS rules forbid a CNAME at the zone apex, so you cannot put a CNAME on the naked `bank.example.com`, only on a subdomain like `www`. Second, every alias lookup through a CNAME on a third-party DNS may be billable and adds a resolution step.

```java
// The two record choices expressed as simple data for clarity
record CnameRecord(String name, String targetName) {}        // name -> another name
record AliasRecord(String name, String awsResourceTarget) {}  // name -> AWS resource, apex allowed

CnameRecord cname = new CnameRecord("www.bank.example.com", "my-alb-123456.ap-south-1.elb.amazonaws.com");
AliasRecord alias = new AliasRecord("bank.example.com", "ALB:my-alb-123456"); // apex OK
```

With a Route 53 alias record, you choose the record type A (or AAAA for IPv6) and set the alias target to the load balancer. Route 53 internally resolves the alias to the load balancer's current IP addresses and returns A records directly to the client, so there is no second lookup visible to the client. Critically, alias records are allowed at the zone apex, so you can map the naked `bank.example.com` straight to the load balancer, which you cannot do with a CNAME. Alias queries to AWS resources are not charged, and if the load balancer's IPs change, Route 53 keeps the alias in sync automatically because it knows the resource, not a frozen IP.

A senior nuance: alias records only work within Route 53 and only to supported AWS targets (ALB, NLB, CloudFront, S3 website, API Gateway, another Route 53 record in the same zone). If your DNS is hosted outside Route 53, you are forced to use a CNAME on a subdomain and you cannot alias the apex, which is a common reason teams migrate their DNS into Route 53.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants customers to reach internet banking at the clean, naked domain `bank.example.com`, with no `www` in front. The service sits behind an Application Load Balancer whose DNS name is long and whose IPs change. A CNAME cannot be used at the naked root domain, so the bank cannot point `bank.example.com` at the load balancer with a CNAME at all. This is exactly what a Route 53 alias record solves: it maps the apex directly to the load balancer.

Problem 2 — The load balancer's IP addresses change over time as AWS scales it. If the bank had hard-coded an IP, customers would suddenly fail to connect when the IP changed. This is exactly why an alias to the resource matters: Route 53 keeps resolving to whatever IPs the load balancer currently has.

We will write a small DNS mapping resolver. `DomainMapper` holds either a CNAME mapping or an alias mapping and resolves a query. A CNAME mapping returns the target name and signals a second lookup is needed, and refuses to be created at the apex. An alias mapping returns the current load balancer IPs directly and is allowed at the apex. The demo shows a successful alias at the apex, and a CNAME being rejected at the apex.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three DNS mapping attempts — an alias for the naked `bank.example.com`, a CNAME for the subdomain `www.bank.example.com`, and a CNAME for the naked `bank.example.com`.

Step 1. The alias for `bank.example.com` is resolved. Because it is an alias to the load balancer resource, Route 53 looks up the load balancer's current IP addresses and returns them directly as A records. The client sees IPs in a single step, and because it is an alias the apex is allowed.

Step 2. The CNAME for `www.bank.example.com` is resolved. It returns the load balancer's DNS name, not an IP. The client must now perform a second DNS lookup on that name to finally obtain an IP. The data went through two hops instead of one.

Step 3. The CNAME for the naked `bank.example.com` is attempted. DNS rules forbid a CNAME at the zone apex, so the mapper throws an exception. The bank cannot use a CNAME here at all, which is the core reason the alias record exists.

Step 4. Over time, AWS changes the load balancer's IP addresses. The alias record keeps returning the new, current IPs automatically because it points to the resource, not to a frozen IP. A hard-coded IP mapping would have broken here.

Step 5. The final output logs the alias returning IPs in one step, the CNAME returning a name needing a second lookup, and the CNAME at apex being rejected.

```
2026-10-29 01:50:00 [INFO] Alias bank.example.com -> A records [13.235.10.42, 13.235.10.77] (one step, apex=true, tracks ALB IPs)
2026-10-29 01:50:00 [INFO] CNAME www.bank.example.com -> my-alb-123456.ap-south-1.elb.amazonaws.com (then resolve that name -> IPs: second lookup)
2026-10-29 01:50:00 [SEVERE] CNAME at apex rejected: CNAME not allowed at zone apex bank.example.com
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To point a domain at an AWS load balancer I create a DNS record in Route 53 that targets the load balancer, and I have two options: a CNAME record or a Route 53 alias record. A load balancer does not give me a fixed IP; it gives me a long DNS name whose underlying IPs change as AWS scales it, so I must map my friendly domain to the resource, never to a hard-coded IP.

A CNAME record maps a name to another name. It works for a subdomain like `www`, but it has two drawbacks. First, DNS rules forbid a CNAME at the zone apex, so I cannot map the naked `bank.example.com` with a CNAME. Second, the client has to do a second DNS lookup to turn the target name into an IP, which adds a resolution step.

A Route 53 alias record is an AWS-specific extension that maps the name straight to the AWS resource. Route 53 resolves it internally to the load balancer's current IP addresses and hands the client A records directly in one step. The three reasons I prefer it for AWS resources are that it is allowed at the zone apex so I can use the clean naked domain, that alias queries to AWS resources are not charged, and that it automatically tracks the load balancer's changing IPs because it knows the resource rather than a frozen address.

At National Bank of India I wanted customers to reach internet banking at the clean `bank.example.com` with no `www`, behind an Application Load Balancer. A CNAME simply cannot sit at that apex, so I used a Route 53 alias A record pointing at the load balancer. That gave customers the naked domain, saved the cost and the extra lookup, and meant that when AWS changed the load balancer's IP addresses our DNS kept resolving correctly with no manual change. The senior point I add is that alias records only work inside Route 53 to supported AWS targets, so if the DNS were hosted elsewhere I would be forced back to a subdomain CNAME, which is a common reason teams move their DNS into Route 53.
